title: The Fall of Nineveh and the Empty Lion's Den
summary: An attacker advances on Nineveh, and the prophet mockingly tells the city to man its defenses. In rapid, vivid poetry the chapter describes red shields, flashing chariots racing through the streets, river gates thrown open, a palace collapsing, and the city's treasure carried off. It ends with a taunt about the lion's den that Assyria filled with prey, and God's declaration that he is against Nineveh.
story: Chapter 1 declared who God is and what he had decided about Nineveh. Chapter 2 shows it happening. The poet places the reader inside the doomed city as the enemy breaks in. Verse 2 pauses the battle to give the reason: God is restoring the splendor of Jacob, the people Assyria had stripped like a vine. The rest of the chapter presents Nineveh's fall as the reversal of Assyria's own history. The empire that plundered nations is plundered; the lion that filled its den with prey finds its den empty. Chapter 3 will add the moral charge sheet, but chapter 2 lets the reader see the collapse first.
historical:
Nineveh fell in 612 BC to a coalition of the Babylonians, under their king Nabopolassar, and the Medes, a people from the Iranian plateau. The Babylonian Chronicle, a series of cuneiform tablets recording the main events of each year, describes a siege lasting several months and the city's capture and plunder. Nineveh was enormous for its time, protected by long walls and a series of gates, with the Tigris on its western side and the Khosr River running through the city. Sennacherib had built canals and dams to supply it with water. Whether flooding played a part in its fall is debated. A Greek historian of the first century BC, Diodorus Siculus, tells of a river that broke down part of the wall, but his account comes centuries later and contains legendary elements. Some scholars think attackers manipulated the city's waterworks; others take Nahum's river gates and draining pool as poetic imagery for collapse.

Nahum wrote before these events, but his poetry fits them closely. Whether the book was composed when Assyria was at its height, after the sack of Thebes around 663 BC, or nearer the end, it presents the city's fall as certain because the LORD has decreed it.
cultural:
Assyrian royal art gives unusual help in reading this chapter. The palaces of Nineveh were lined with carved stone reliefs showing the king's campaigns: siege ramps, chariots, captives led away, and cities burning. Many of these panels are now in the British Museum, including Sennacherib's depiction of the siege of Lachish in Judah and Ashurbanipal's famous scenes of royal lion hunts. Assyrian kings described themselves in lion imagery and staged lion hunts as displays of power. Nahum's lion's den in verses 11 and 12 turns that imagery against them: the royal lion hauled prey home to its cubs, and now the den is empty.

The details of the attack reflect ancient warfare. Shields reddened (perhaps painted, covered in copper, or stained) and soldiers in scarlet were meant to intimidate. Chariots with metal fittings flashed in the sun, and spears of cypress wood were brandished before battle. In verse 7, captured women moan like doves and beat their breasts, the gesture of mourning. The word translated it is decreed in verse 7 is obscure in Hebrew; older English versions, including the King James, took it as a name, Huzzab, possibly a queen, while most modern translations read it as a verb.
literary: Nahum 2 is some of the most vivid battle poetry in the Old Testament. Its lines are short and packed with verbs of motion, and the Hebrew uses sound effects that translation cannot fully carry, especially in verse 10, where three nearly rhyming words describe the city as emptied, desolate, and laid waste. The chapter opens with sarcastic commands to the defenders (verse 1), then breaks off for a theological aside about Jacob (verse 2), before plunging into the attack (verses 3 to 7). The scene of flight and plunder (verses 8 to 10) uses the image of a pool draining away. The final section (verses 11 to 13) switches to an extended metaphor of lions, asking where the den has gone, and closes with God's direct speech, the formula Behold, I am against you, which returns in 3:5.

outline.t: The attacker advances: guard the fortress
The LORD restores the splendor of Jacob
The river gates open and the palace falls
Flight and plunder: the city emptied

doctrines.note: Nineveh's fall is presented as God's act (verse 13), even though human armies carry it out. The punishment mirrors the crime: the plunderer is plundered and the predator's den is emptied.
God works through the rise and fall of nations, using the Babylonians and Medes to accomplish his decree without approving everything they do. History is not random; it answers to the LORD of Hosts.
Verse 2 gives the reason behind the battle: God restoring the splendor of Jacob and Israel. His judgment on Assyria is bound up with his faithfulness to the people he had chosen.

words.note: Shuv, to turn or return, here in the sense of restore. God will restore the splendor of Jacob. The verb is one of the great words of the prophets, used for Israel's repentance and for God's restoring of their fortunes. Its placement in the middle of a battle scene shows that the purpose of Nineveh's fall is the recovery of God's people.

Aryeh, lion, used three times in verses 11 and 12. The lion was the favorite image of Assyrian royal power. Nahum's extended lion metaphor turns the empire's self-image into its epitaph: the predator that stocked its den with prey now has no den at all.

Bazaz, to plunder or seize as spoil. The cry in verse 9 to plunder the silver and gold reverses Assyria's own history, since its wealth came largely from tribute and loot taken from other nations. What was gathered by violence is scattered by violence.

Tsava, hosts or armies, in the title LORD of Hosts. The title presents God as commander of heavenly and earthly armies. Nineveh has chariots and warriors, but the one who says I am against you commands forces greater than any empire.

christ: Nahum 2 does not speak of a coming Messiah, and any link to Christ is thematic. The chapter shows God acting to restore his people by overthrowing the power that had oppressed them, a pattern that runs from the exodus through the prophets to the New Testament. Mary's song in Luke 1 praises the God who has brought down rulers from their thrones and lifted up the humble, and Colossians 2:15 speaks of Christ disarming the powers and authorities and triumphing over them. The New Testament does not present Jesus leading armies against earthly empires; it presents him defeating the deeper powers of sin and death, and it looks to his return to judge the nations in righteousness. Nahum's picture of a violent empire emptied and silenced, the voices of its messengers no longer heard, is one early chapter in the Bible's long testimony that no oppressive power has the last word.

hard.q: Is it right for Scripture to describe the plunder of a city and the grief of its captives with such apparent satisfaction?
hard.a: The poetry of Nahum 2 does not pause to mourn Nineveh, and that troubles many readers. Several things help. The chapter is written from the perspective of Assyria's victims, who had suffered precisely these things at Assyrian hands; Assyria's own reliefs celebrate burning cities and deported captives. The poem shows the terrible logic of violence coming home. It also ascribes the judgment to God rather than inviting Judah to take revenge. Some interpreters add that the prophets elsewhere show grief even over enemy nations (Isaiah 15:5, Jeremiah 48:31), and that Jonah records God's compassion for Nineveh's people and animals. These texts together suggest that God's judgment is real and just, while his desire is not for anyone's destruction. Readers who feel the weight of the scene are not wrong to feel it; the book wants them to see what empire costs.

questions: The empire that plundered others is itself plundered. Where have you seen the harm people cause return to them?
Assyria described itself as a lion. What images do nations, institutions, or people use to project power today, and what does Nahum suggest about them?
Verse 2 says God's purpose in the battle is to restore his people. How might it change the way you see hard events to ask what God might be restoring through them?
